native_templates.prompt_template: Find the mean of {v1}, {v2}, {center}, {v4}, and {v5}.
native_templates.explanation_template:
The deviations from {center} cancel in pairs: -{a}, -{b}, 0, +{b}, +{a}.
The sum is 5 * {center}, so the mean is {center}.

work.prompt: Show an equivalent numerical expression on each line, ending with the final value.

native_templates.prompt_template: The mean of {a}, {b}, {c}, {d}, and x is {mean}. Find x.
native_templates.explanation_template:
A mean of {mean} for five values requires a total of {5 * mean}.
The four known values total {a + b + c + d}.
So x = {5 * mean} - {a + b + c + d} = {missing}.

work.prompt: Write a mean equation containing x, then solve it one equivalent equation per line.

native_templates.prompt_template: The values are already ordered: {v1}, {v2}, {v3}, {v4}, {v5}. What is the median?
native_templates.explanation_template:
There are five ordered values, so the median is the third value.
The third value is {v3}.

native_templates.prompt_template: The values are already ordered: {v1}, {v2}, {v3}, {v4}, {v5}, {v6}. What is the median?
native_templates.explanation_template:
With six ordered values, average the third and fourth.
({v3} + {v4}) / 2 = {median}.

work.prompt: Show an equivalent numerical expression on each line, ending with the final value.

native_templates.prompt_template: Find the mode of {low}, {mode}, {high}, {mode}, {far}, {mode}.
native_templates.explanation_template: The value {mode} appears three times. Every other value appears once, so the mode is {mode}.

native_templates.prompt_template: Find the range of the dataset {low}, {low_plus}, {middle}, {near_high}, {high}.
native_templates.explanation_template:
Range = maximum - minimum.
{high} - ({low}) = {spread}.

work.prompt: Show an equivalent numerical expression on each line, ending with the final value.

native_templates.prompt_template: A course grade uses score {score1} with weight {weight1} and score {score2} with weight {weight2}. Treat the weights as relative frequencies. What is the weighted mean?
native_templates.explanation_template:
Multiply each score by its weight, add, then divide by the total weight.
({score1}*{weight1} + {score2}*{weight2}) / {weight_total} = {weighted_mean}.

work.prompt: Show the weighted total and divide by the total weight.

native_templates.prompt_template: Using the median-of-halves convention, find the IQR of the ordered data 2, 4, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13, 18.
native_templates.explanation_template:
The lower-half median is Q1 = (4 + 5)/2 = 4.5.
The upper-half median is Q3 = (11 + 13)/2 = 12.
IQR = 12 - 4.5 = 7.5.

work.prompt: Find Q1 and Q3, then subtract to obtain the IQR.

native_templates.prompt_template: A dataset has Q1 = 10 and Q3 = 18. Which listed value is an outlier under the 1.5*IQR rule?
native_templates.explanation_template: IQR = 18 - 10 = 8. The fences are 10 - 12 = -2 and 18 + 12 = 30. Only 33 lies outside the fences.

native_templates.prompt_template: The two dot plots show Dataset A = 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and Dataset B = 2, 3, 4, 5, 18. Which statistic is 4 for both datasets?
native_templates.explanation_template: The middle ordered value is 4 in both datasets, so both medians are 4. Dataset B's mean is larger because of 18.

skills.name: Distributions, histograms, and box plots
skills.description: Read and compare distributions using frequency, relative frequency, histograms, box plots, MAD, variance, and standard deviation.
skills.theory: A graph of a distribution should make shape, center, spread, and unusual features visible. Frequency is a count and relative frequency is a fraction or percent. Histograms group quantitative values into adjacent bins; skew is named for the direction of the long tail. Box plots show minimum, Q1, median, Q3, and maximum. MAD averages absolute distances from the mean. Population variance averages squared deviations from the mean, and population standard deviation is its square root. Adding a constant leaves SD unchanged; multiplying by c multiplies SD by |c|. Compare distributions with center, spread, shape, and outliers together.

skills.name: Scatter plots, correlation, and residuals
skills.description: Describe bivariate association, use fitted lines, calculate and interpret residuals, and distinguish correlation from causation.
skills.theory: Bivariate data record two variables for each observational unit. Describe association by direction, form, strength, and unusual features. Correlation r measures linear association from -1 to 1; r near zero can coexist with strong nonlinear association. Correlation does not prove causation. A fitted line y_hat=mx+b predicts the response; interpolation stays within the observed range and extrapolation extends outside it. Residual=observed-predicted. Random residual scatter supports a linear form; curvature signals missing structure. High-leverage points can be influential and should be investigated rather than automatically deleted.

applications.description: Fitted lines support transparent predictions within a measured range.

applications.description: Residual plots reveal patterns a model fails to explain.

applications.title: Data ethics
applications.description: Separating association from causal claims prevents misleading conclusions.

skills.name: Normal distributions and z-scores
skills.description: Interpret normal density curves, z-scores, empirical-rule areas and standardized comparisons.
skills.theory: A normal distribution is a continuous symmetric bell-shaped model determined by mean μ and standard deviation σ. Probability is area, and an exact point has probability zero. Standardize with z=(x-μ)/σ and reverse with x=μ+zσ. The empirical rule gives about 68%,95%,99.7% within 1,2,3 SD. z-scores compare relative standing across scales. A normal model is questionable for strong skew, multimodality, extreme outliers, or hard boundaries near the center.

examples.prompt: A battery life is 12.25 hours, with mean 10 and SD 1.5. Find its z-score.
examples.solution: A battery life is normal with mean 10 hours and SD 1.5. For 12.25 hours, z=(12.25-10)/1.5=1.5.
examples.explanation: The battery lasts 1.5 standard deviations above the mean.

examples.prompt: For a normal model with mean 70 and SD 8, estimate P(62<X<78).
examples.solution: For N(70,8), P(62<X<78) is approximately the area between z=-1 and z=1, about 0.68.
examples.explanation: Standardize both bounds, then use the empirical rule or a normal calculator.

skills.name: Sampling distributions and standard error
skills.description: Distinguish parameters/statistics, model sampling variability, calculate standard errors and apply CLT conditions.
skills.theory: Inference starts from sampling variability. A population parameter is fixed but unknown; a sample statistic varies across random samples. Sampling distributions describe this variation. E(x-bar)=μ and E(p-hat)=p. SE(x-bar)=σ/sqrt(n), SE(p-hat)=sqrt[p(1-p)/n]. Quadrupling n halves SE. Check randomization, independence/10% condition, and normal/large-count conditions. The Central Limit Theorem makes the distribution of sample means more nearly normal as n grows. Large n reduces random variation but does not repair selection or measurement bias.

examples.prompt: A population has SD 12 and samples have size 36. Find the standard error of the sample mean.
examples.solution: If population SD is 12 and n=36, SE(x-bar)=12/sqrt(36)=2.
examples.explanation: The sampling mean varies less than individual observations.

examples.prompt: Assume a normal population has mean 50 and SD 10. Describe the center and approximate 95% spread of means for n=25.
examples.solution: The sampling mean is 50 and SE=10/sqrt(25)=2; about 95% of means lie within 50±2(2), or (46,54).
examples.explanation: Center stays at the population mean while standard error controls spread.

skills.name: Confidence intervals and margin of error
skills.description: Construct and interpret confidence intervals, margins, conditions and sample-size plans.
skills.theory: A confidence interval is estimate ± margin of error, with margin=critical value×standard error. A 95% confidence procedure captures the fixed parameter in about 95% of repeated samples under its conditions. Higher confidence widens intervals; larger n narrows them at a square-root rate. Mean intervals with known σ use x-bar±z*σ/sqrt(n). Introductory proportion intervals use p-hat±z*sqrt[p-hat(1-p-hat)/n]. Check randomization, independence/10%, shape or count conditions, and nonsampling bias separately. Sample-size planning solves the margin formula and rounds upward.

examples.prompt: A sample mean is 50 with known standard error 1.5. Construct a 95% confidence interval.
examples.solution: A sample mean 50 with known SE 1.5 gives a 95% interval 50 plus or minus 1.96(1.5)=(47.06,52.94).
examples.explanation: The interval is a plausible range for the population mean produced by the procedure.

examples.prompt: How does quadrupling sample size affect a margin of error? Explain why.
examples.solution: To cut a margin of error from 4 to 2, quadruple the sample size because margin varies as 1/sqrt(n).
examples.explanation: Precision improves through larger samples, while confidence level also changes width.

skills.name: Hypothesis tests, p-values, and power
skills.description: Form hypotheses, calculate test statistics/p-values, decisions, errors, power and practical significance.
skills.theory: A significance test measures compatibility of data with a specified null model. Hypotheses concern population parameters. Test statistic=(estimate-null value)/(SE under H0). The p-value is the probability under H0/model of a statistic at least as extreme in the direction(s) of Ha; it is not P(H0). Choose alpha before analysis. Reject when p≤alpha; otherwise fail to reject. Type I error rejects a true H0; Type II misses a real alternative; power is probability of rejection under a specified alternative. Report effect size, interval, practical importance, design, and limitations.

examples.prompt: A test has p-value 0.03 and significance level 0.05. State the decision and its meaning.
examples.solution: With p-value 0.03 and alpha 0.05, reject H0; the evidence is statistically significant at the 5% level.
examples.explanation: A p-value is the chance of results this extreme or more under H0, not the probability H0 is true.

examples.prompt: Explain how increasing sample size affects power when the effect is fixed.
examples.solution: For an effect size 0.5 with SE 0.2, the standardized signal is 2.5; increasing n lowers SE and raises power.
examples.explanation: Power is the probability of rejecting a false null under a specified alternative.

skills.name: Student’s t distributions and one-sample t inference
skills.description: Use Student t distributions for one-sample mean intervals/tests when sigma is unknown.
skills.theory: When population standard deviation is unknown, replace sigma with sample s and use Student’s t. One-sample t statistic=(xbar-mu0)/(s/sqrt(n)), df=n-1. t distributions are symmetric with heavier tails at small df and approach normal as df grows. the t-distribution calculator returns lower-tail probability. One-sample t interval=xbar±t*s/sqrt(n). Check randomization/independence and, for small n, roughly normal data without severe outliers.

examples.prompt: A sample has n=16, mean 52, SD 8. Test a population mean of 48 using a t statistic.
examples.solution: With n=16, x-bar=52, s=8, and H0 mean 48, t=(52-48)/(8/sqrt(16))=2 with df=15.
examples.explanation: Use the t distribution because the population SD is estimated by s.

examples.prompt: Using mean 52, SE 2, df 15, and t*=2.131, construct a 95% interval.
examples.solution: For a 95% interval with df=15 and t*=2.131, mean 52 plus or minus 2.131(2) gives (47.74,56.26).
examples.explanation: The t critical value accounts for extra uncertainty in a small sample.

skills.name: Comparing two means and matched pairs
skills.description: Compare independent population means and paired mean differences with t methods.
skills.theory: Comparing two means depends on design. Independent groups use difference xbar1-xbar2 with SE from both samples and a Welch-type t reference. Matched pairs reduce each pair to one difference and use a one-sample t method on the differences. Confidence intervals and tests use the same parameter and consistent subtraction direction. Check independence, outliers/shape, and distinguish random assignment (causation) from random sampling (generalization).

examples.prompt: Before-after differences are 2, 4, and 3. Find the mean paired difference.
examples.solution: Paired differences before-after are 2,4,3, so mean difference=(2+4+3)/3=3.
examples.explanation: Analyze within-person differences when observations are naturally matched.

examples.prompt: Two independent group means differ by 3 with SE 1.2. Find the standardized statistic.
examples.solution: Group means 18 and 15 with SE of difference 1.2 give t=3/1.2=2.5.
examples.explanation: For independent groups, standardize the difference in means by its standard error.

skills.description: Construct/test one and two population proportions, pooled tests, intervals and conditions.
skills.theory: Inference for proportions uses sample counts and normal approximations. One-proportion tests use null p0 in the standard error, while confidence intervals use p-hat. Two-proportion confidence intervals combine unpooled sample variances; tests of p1=p2 use a pooled estimate. A normal-distribution calculator provides tail probabilities and critical values. Check randomization, independence/10%, and success-failure counts; report risk differences and scope, not p-values alone.

examples.prompt: In 80 trials there are 44 successes. Find the sample proportion and its standard error.
examples.solution: In 80 trials with 44 successes, p-hat=44/80=0.55 and SE=sqrt(.55(.45)/80)=0.0557.
examples.explanation: The sample proportion estimates the population proportion with sampling uncertainty.

examples.prompt: Using p-hat=.55 and SE=.0557, construct an approximate 95% interval.
examples.solution: A 95% interval is .55 plus or minus 1.96(.0557)=(.441,.659).
examples.explanation: State the interval in proportion or percentage units and check success-failure conditions.

skills.name: Chi-square goodness-of-fit tests
skills.description: Compare observed categorical counts with a specified population distribution.
skills.theory: Chi-square goodness-of-fit compares observed categorical counts with expected counts from a specified null distribution. E_i=np_i, statistic Σ(O-E)^2/E, df=k-1 when no parameters are estimated. Tests are right-tailed; use stable `chi_square_sf`. Check independent counts and adequate expected counts. Significant global fit evidence does not identify every differing category or establish causation; inspect standardized residuals and report effect/context.

examples.prompt: Observed category counts are 18 and 22; expected counts are 20 and 20. Find chi-square.
examples.solution: Observed counts 18,22 and expected counts 20,20 give chi-square=(18-20)^2/20+(22-20)^2/20=0.4.
examples.explanation: Small discrepancy means the data are close to the proposed categorical distribution.

examples.prompt: A goodness-of-fit test has four categories and no estimated parameters. Find its degrees of freedom.
examples.solution: For four categories with no parameters estimated, df=4-1=3.
examples.explanation: Degrees of freedom determine the reference chi-square distribution for the goodness-of-fit test.

skills.name: Chi-square tests for two-way tables
skills.description: Test independence/homogeneity in contingency tables using expected counts, cell contributions and right-tail p-values.
skills.theory: Chi-square tests for two-way tables compare observed cells with independence-model expected counts E=(row total)(column total)/grand total. Independence and homogeneity use the same calculation but differ in sampling design and conclusion. df=(r-1)(c-1). Use the right-tail `chi_square_sf`; inspect cell contributions and standardized residuals. Check independent observations and expected counts, and do not convert association into a causal claim without design support.

examples.prompt: A table cell has row total 40, column total 30, and grand total 100. Find its expected count under independence.
examples.solution: In a 2x2 table with row total 40, column total 30, and grand total 100, expected cell count=(40)(30)/100=12.
examples.explanation: Expected counts represent independence while preserving the margins.

examples.prompt: A two-way chi-square statistic is 9.6 with one degree of freedom. How should association be assessed?
examples.solution: For chi-square=9.6 with df=1, the right-tail p-value is approximately 0.00195. Since .00195<.05, reject independence and conclude evidence of association.
examples.explanation: A two-way chi-square test evaluates association, not causation.

skills.name: Inference for a linear regression slope
skills.description: Use Student t procedures to test/estimate population regression slope and diagnose assumptions.
skills.theory: Regression inference estimates/tests a population slope β1 using t=(b1-β10)/SE_b1 with df=n-2 in simple linear regression. Use the t-distribution calculator for one/two-sided p-values and b1±t*SE for intervals. Check linearity, independence, roughly normal residuals for small samples, constant variance, and influential cases. A slope association is not automatically causal; study design controls causal and generalization claims. Matching confidence intervals and two-sided tests correspond.

examples.solution: A 95% slope interval with b=.8 and t*=2.1 is .8 plus or minus 2.1(.2)=(.38,1.22).
examples.explanation: Interpret the interval in response units per one predictor unit.

skills.name: One-way ANOVA and F tests
skills.description: Compare three or more independent population means with variance decomposition, F tests and effect sizes.
skills.theory: One-way ANOVA compares three or more independent population means through variance decomposition. H0 states all means equal; Ha says not all equal. SS_total=SS_between+SS_within, df_between=k-1, df_within=N-k, mean squares divide sums by df, and F=MS_between/MS_within. Use the right-tail F-distribution calculator. Check independence, shape/outliers, and similar spreads; a significant global result does not say every pair differs. Report effect size eta² and use multiplicity-aware follow-up comparisons.

examples.prompt: Three groups contain 18 observations. SSbetween=60 and SSwithin=90. Find the ANOVA F statistic.
examples.explanation: The between-group mean square is five times the within-group mean square, so group means vary substantially relative to within-group noise.

examples.prompt: An ANOVA returns p=0.01 at significance 0.05. What can you conclude and what follow-up is needed?
examples.solution: If an ANOVA p-value is .01 at alpha .05, reject equal means, then use planned pairwise comparisons to locate differences.
examples.explanation: The omnibus test establishes that at least one mean differs; it does not identify which one.

skills.name: Multiple linear regression and partial effects
skills.description: Interpret/test partial slopes, indicators, interactions, confounding, multicollinearity and F tests.
skills.theory: Multiple regression models a quantitative response using several predictors. Each partial slope describes fitted mean change for one predictor holding the others fixed. Indicator variables encode categories; interactions let effects depend on another predictor. Confounding and multicollinearity can change coefficients and standard errors. Individual coefficients use t inference with df=n-p-1; overall/nested model questions use F and the F-distribution calculator. R² never decreases with added predictors, while adjusted R² penalizes complexity. Diagnostics, extrapolation, influence, and causal design remain essential.

examples.prompt: In y=10+2x1-.5x2, interpret the coefficient of x1 while x2 is fixed.
examples.solution: In y=10+2x1-.5x2, increasing x1 by 1 changes predicted y by 2 while holding x2 fixed.
examples.explanation: A multiple-regression coefficient is a partial effect conditional on the other predictors.

examples.prompt: A regression coefficient is .6 with SE .15. Find its t statistic and interpret the evidence.
examples.solution: With n=50 and 3 predictors, df=50-3-1=46 and t=.6/.15=4. Using t*=2.013, the 95% interval is .6±2.013(.15)=(.298,.902), supporting a positive partial association.
examples.explanation: Use coefficient units and uncertainty when interpreting a fitted model.

skills.name: Bootstrap and randomization-based inference
skills.description: Build bootstrap intervals and randomization tests that match design, dependence and null mechanism.
skills.theory: Resampling approximates sampling or null distributions by repeatedly resampling observed data according to a justified mechanism. A nonparametric bootstrap draws n observations with replacement and estimates standard errors or percentile intervals from the bootstrap statistic distribution. Randomization tests recreate a null assignment/exchangeability mechanism; empirical p-values can use (r+1)/(B+1). Resampling must preserve pairs, clusters, blocks, or time dependence. More repetitions reduce Monte Carlo noise but do not add observational information or fix bias. Resampling is not assumption-free.

examples.prompt: Observed values are 2, 4, 4, 7, 7, and a bootstrap resample is 2, 2, 4, 7, 7. Find the resample mean.
examples.solution: The resample mean is (2+2+4+7+7)/5=22/5=4.4; repeat many resamples to form a bootstrap distribution.
examples.explanation: Resampling approximates the sampling variability of a statistic.

skills.name: Probability models and sample spaces
skills.description: Build sample spaces, calculate theoretical and experimental probabilities, use complements, simulation, and area models.
skills.theory: Probability assigns numbers from 0 to 1 to events. Outcomes form a complete sample space, and events are subsets of it. For equally likely outcomes, P(event)=favorable/total. Complements obey P(not A)=1-P(A). Multi-stage sample spaces use organized lists, trees, or tables; independent choice counts multiply. Experimental probability is observed successes divided by trials and approaches model probability in long runs without matching it exactly. Uniform geometric probability is favorable area divided by total area. Always check completeness, equal-likelihood assumptions, and that the result lies from 0 to 1.

examples.prompt: Two fair dice are rolled. Find the probability that their sum is 7.
examples.solution: Two fair dice have 36 ordered outcomes and 6 sum to 7, so P(sum=7)=6/36=1/6.
examples.explanation: Count favorable outcomes in the complete equally likely sample space.

examples.prompt: A spinner has 8 equally likely equal-size sectors, 3 favorable. Find the event and complement probabilities.
examples.solution: A spinner has 3 favorable sectors out of 8, so P(event)=3/8 and P(not event)=5/8.

skills.name: Compound and conditional probability
skills.description: Combine events with addition/multiplication rules, conditional probability, independence, tables, trees and Bayes rule.
skills.theory: Compound probability distinguishes union, intersection, conditional probability, independence, and complements. P(A or B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A and B). Conditional probability changes the denominator: P(A|B)=P(A and B)/P(B). Multiplication gives P(A and B)=P(A)P(B|A); for independence this becomes P(A)P(B). Tree diagrams multiply along a path and add across qualifying paths. Without replacement changes later probabilities. Bayes reasoning reverses a condition by dividing the relevant joint path by all paths producing the observed event.

examples.prompt: A bag has 3 red and 2 blue counters. Find the probability of drawing two red without replacement.

examples.prompt: Given P(A)=1/2, P(B|A)=2/3, and P(B)=1/3, find P(A and B) and P(A|B).
examples.solution: If P(A)=1/2 and P(B|A)=2/3, then P(A and B)=1/3; if P(B)=1/3, P(A|B)=1.
examples.explanation: Multiplication finds a joint path and Bayes reasoning reverses the condition.

skills.name: Discrete random variables and expected value
skills.description: Validate discrete probability distributions, calculate expected value, compare risk, and analyze fair games.
skills.theory: A discrete random variable assigns numerical values to countable outcomes. A valid probability distribution has probabilities from 0 to 1 that sum to 1. Expected value is the probability-weighted average E(X)=ΣxP(X=x), interpreted as a long-run average. Distinguish gross payout from net payoff after cost. A fair game has expected net payoff zero. For n Bernoulli trials with success probability p, expected successes=np. Linearity gives E(aX+b)=aE(X)+b. Equal expected values can hide very different variability and risk.

skills.name: Counting principles, permutations, and combinations
skills.description: Count multistage outcomes and distinguish ordered arrangements from unordered selections.
skills.theory: Counting begins by defining what one outcome records. The fundamental counting principle multiplies choices across successive stages. If repetition is allowed in k positions with n symbols, there are n^k strings. Factorials count arrangements. Permutations count ordered selections nPr=n!/(n-r)!, while combinations count unordered selections nCr=n!/[r!(n-r)!]. Repeated identical objects require division by repeated factorials. “At least one” events are often easiest by complement counting.

examples.prompt: How many ordered 3-letter arrangements can be made from 5 distinct letters when letters cannot repeat?

examples.explanation: Use permutations when order changes the outcome.

skills.name: Binomial probability distributions
skills.description: Recognize binomial settings and calculate probabilities, mean and spread.
skills.theory: A binomial random variable counts successes in a fixed number n of independent binary trials with constant success probability p. Check BINS: Binary, Independent, Number fixed, Same p. P(X=k)=nCk p^k(1-p)^(n-k). “At least one” is often a complement. Mean=np, variance=np(1-p), SD=sqrt(np(1-p)). Sampling without replacement is not exactly binomial because p changes.

skills.name: Angles, bearings, and degree measure
skills.description: Measure rotation in degrees, distinguish direction from orientation, and use bearings as angular descriptions of location.
skills.theory:
An angle measures rotation between two rays that share a vertex. A full turn is 360°, a half turn is 180°, and a quarter turn is 90°. Degree measure is not a length: two arcs can have different lengths while subtending the same angle if their radii differ. This distinction becomes essential when degrees are used to describe positions on Earth.

Angles may be measured clockwise or counterclockwise from a reference direction. In standard coordinate geometry, angles are commonly measured counterclockwise from the positive x-axis. A bearing uses a different convention: it is measured clockwise from north and written with three digits, such as 045° or 270°. Converting between conventions requires identifying the reference ray before doing arithmetic.

Compass directions provide useful benchmarks. North is 000° (or 360°), east is 090°, south is 180°, and west is 270°. A bearing of 135° points southeast because it lies halfway between east and south. The opposite, or reciprocal, bearing differs by 180° after wrapping the result into the interval from 000° to 359°.

Angular separation is the smaller rotation between two directions unless a problem explicitly asks for signed rotation. For bearings a and b, compute |a − b|. If that difference exceeds 180°, subtract it from 360°. Thus the smaller separation between 350° and 020° is 30°, not 330°.

Degrees can be divided into 60 minutes, and each minute into 60 seconds. The notation 42° 30′ 00″ is 42.5° because 30/60 = 0.5. Decimal degrees are easier to calculate with, while degrees–minutes–seconds remain common in navigation and surveying. Always label which representation you are using.

The central habit is to separate three questions: What is the reference direction? Which way is rotation measured? Do we want signed rotation or the smaller angular separation? Once those are explicit, bearings and geographic coordinates become ordinary, checkable geometry.

skills.name: Circles, arcs, and angular distance
skills.description: Relate central angles to arc length and use radians or degree fractions to measure distance along a circle.
skills.theory:
A central angle has its vertex at the centre of a circle. It intercepts an arc, and the arc’s share of the circumference is the same as the angle’s share of a full turn. In degrees, s = (θ/360°)·2πr, where s is arc length, θ is the central angle, and r is radius.

Radians express the same relationship more directly. One radian is the angle that intercepts an arc equal in length to the radius. Because a full circumference is 2πr, a full turn is 2π radians. When θ is in radians, arc length is s = rθ. Never place a degree value directly into s = rθ without converting it.

Conversion follows from 180° = π radians. Multiply degrees by π/180 to obtain radians, and multiply radians by 180/π to obtain degrees. Familiar benchmarks are 30° = π/6, 45° = π/4, 60° = π/3, 90° = π/2, and 180° = π.

Angular distance and linear distance answer different questions. Two points separated by 10° on a small circle are closer together than two points separated by 10° on a large circle. On a sphere, the same angular separation also represents different east–west distances at different latitudes because circles of latitude shrink toward the poles.

The shortest route constrained to the circumference of a circle is the minor arc when the central angle is at most 180°. On a sphere the analogue is a segment of a great circle—a circle whose centre is the sphere’s centre. This is why long-distance routes can look curved on common flat maps while still following the shortest surface path.

Estimation is a useful safeguard. A 90° arc must be one quarter of a circumference; a 1° arc must be 1/360. If a calculation violates that scale, check units and whether the angle was converted correctly.

skills.name: Spherical coordinates and great-circle models
skills.description: Extend coordinate reasoning from a plane to a sphere and model angular separation, meridians, parallels, and great-circle distance.
skills.theory:
A flat coordinate plane uses perpendicular x- and y-axes. A sphere has no single flat grid that covers its surface without distortion, so positions are described by angles. Geographic latitude measures angular displacement north or south of the equatorial plane. Longitude measures angular displacement east or west around Earth from a chosen prime meridian.

Parallels are circles of constant latitude. The equator is the largest parallel and a great circle. Other parallels are smaller circles because their planes do not pass through Earth’s centre. Meridians are halves of great circles joining the poles. Opposite meridians together form a complete great circle.

Latitude ranges from 90° south to 90° north. Longitude is commonly represented from 180° west to 180° east, or equivalently from 0° to 360°. These conventions create wrap-around: 179°E and 179°W are only 2° apart across the antimeridian, not 358° apart.

North–south distance is comparatively simple in a spherical model because one degree of latitude always spans the same central angle on a meridian. East–west distance per degree of longitude shrinks with latitude. At latitude φ, the radius of the parallel is approximately R cos φ, so one degree of longitude spans about (πR/180) cos φ.

For general pairs of points, their longitude and latitude differences do not form an ordinary Cartesian right triangle over large distances. A great-circle calculation accounts for spherical geometry. The haversine formula is numerically stable: a = sin²(Δφ/2) + cos φ₁ cos φ₂ sin²(Δλ/2), c = 2 atan2(√a, √(1−a)), and distance d = Rc. Angles must be in radians.

Earth is not a perfect sphere. Precise surveying uses an ellipsoid and an explicit geodetic datum. A spherical calculation is a model whose adequacy depends on purpose: excellent for conceptual and many regional estimates, insufficient for boundary surveying or high-precision navigation.

The essential bridge is conceptual. Latitude and longitude are not arbitrary labels placed on a flat map; they are angular coordinates on a curved surface. Any flat display is a projection of that geometry and therefore introduces structured distortion.
